guion_largo.texto:
This temple holds something that is almost never seen at Chichén Itzá: color.

The Temple of the Great Tables lies north of the Temple of the Warriors. It was discovered during the excavations of nineteen ninety-three and ninety-four, coordinated by Peter Schmidt. It is a pyramidal structure with a base of four tiers and a small shrine at the top. Its main facade faces west, and it is the only access.

Most remarkable are its pilasters. They still preserve their painted finish almost entirely, that is, the original paint. So far, only two sides of each pilaster have been left exposed. In most of the neighboring plaza, by contrast, the pilasters of the Group of the Thousand Columns and of the Market lost almost all of their polychromy.

The decoration includes two serpents at the ends of the balustrades, reliefs of warriors in the center, and a table held up by Atlantean figures at the northeast corner. That is where the name comes from. These are altars resting on small male figures, with their arms raised. In the first vault, a mural with a serpent was found.

Do not confuse this building with the Temple of the Little Tables, which another study places near the Palace of the Sculpted Columns.

When you finish, continue to the next stop on your tour.

texto.pregunta: Myth: All the buildings at Chichén Itzá were made of gray stone, without color.
texto.respuesta: Reality: There was paint. In this temple, the pilasters preserve their painted finish almost completely, something uncommon at the site.
